LDS [21,22]. These studies involved the tensile deformation behaviour

[21] have reported that B2 plays a significant role in deformation re-
sponse. Strain incompatibility arises due to microstructural heterogene-
ity, leading to increased back stress in the ??-matrix. Both the back
stress-induced hardening and forest dislocation hardening contribute
to the high strain hardening ability of the alloy. On the contrary, Kim
[22] showed experimentally and argued that B2 has a limited role in the
deformation response of LDS alloys. It was reported that the ??-matrix
composition plays a dominant role in the strain hardening. In addition,
it was documented that the B2 phase in stringer morphology can afect
forming by reducing ductility in transverse direction [23]. It is worth
mentioning that the introduction of cold rolling followed by annealing
heat treatment modifies the stringer orientation and its characteristics
From the industrial processing point of view, the as-cast ingots/slabs
undergo hot rolling practice before cold rolling (and annealing) to pro-
duce required sheets for forming any structural component. Thus, there
is a necessity for understanding the efect of alloy chemistry on the mi-
crostructural evolution from casting to hot rolling and subsequently the
role of the constituents on deformation behaviour of the hot-rolled LDS
alloys before cold rolling. However, there are limited studies on defor-
mation behaviour and the evolution of deformed microstructure in the
hot-rolled LDS. This literature gap highlights the need for a systematic
investigation to evaluate the alloy chemistry and the role of the resultant
secondary phases such as ??-carbide, B2 stringers/particles on deforma-
tion behaviour of hot-rolled Fe-Mn-Al-C-(Ni) based LDS alloys.
In view of the aforementioned literature gaps, the present study
was undertaken with specific objective of investigating the role of mi-
crostructural constituents, the B2 phase in particular, on the strength-
ductility combination observed in the as-hot rolled plates of Ni-free and
Ni containing LDS. Three low-density steel alloy compositions, which
are known to produce B2-free and B2 containing ??-matrix, such as
28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni, and 15Mn5Ni alloys with nearly constant Al and
C contents, were melted, and the ingots were subsequently hot-rolled.
The mechanical properties were evaluated through hardness (macro &
nanoindentation) and tensile testing at room temperature on the hot-
rolled alloys. The role of secondary phases on the deformation charac-
teristics of LDS was deconvoluted by conducting detailed transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) in conjunction with automated crystal ori-
entation mapping (ACOM).

loys after tensile testing. The 15Mn5Ni alloy showed a distinctive frac-
ture surface topography from that of the other two alloys. The insets in
each image show one-half of the failed tensile specimens. Both 28Mn0Ni

4.2.3. Strain hardening and ductility
The role of B2 phase on the strain hardening behaviour of LDS al-
loys has become a debatable topic in the recent past, and as highlighted
in introduction section there exists two opposing view-points [21][22].
The mechanism proposed by Yang et al. [21] was based on the strain
and stress partitioning between ?? and B2 phases. They reported that de-
formation of B2 phase starts at a later stage of deformation
( \varepsilon \sim 0 . 0 8 )
but strain hardens faster than ?? phase. The transient plateau in the flow
curve was thus attributed to this composite deformation. Subsequent
back stress generation and forest hardening in the ??-matrix in the pres-
ence of B2 led to higher hardening rate observed in the B2 containing
alloy. On the contrary, Kim [22] emphasised that the dislocation sub-
structure evolution in austenite is governed by alloy composition, which
plays a primary role, and B2 has a secondary role in strain hardening.
Since there was no plateau in the stress-strain curve, Kim [22] also pro-
posed that the transient portion of the flow curve does not originate
due to the stress/strain partitioning; rather, it may be an indication of
Lüder band formation. The absence of any noticeable plateaus in the
stress-strain curves of all the three alloys (Fig. 5a) supports the argu
ment given by Kim [22].
The slip activity in LDS alloy depends on the nature of ??/B2 interface.
Favourably orientated soft B2 grains (with ??-grains) present in stringers
can deform simultaneously through slip transfer near yield, whereas,
slip transfer restriction across non-favourable

the yield strength and afects subsequent strain hardening behaviour.
It was observed that the strain hardening of both the alloys 28Mn0Ni
and 15Mn5Ni mostly proceeds by planar glide and associated slip band
refinement (Fig. 8). Similar dynamic slip band refinement has been re-
ported in recent studies on B2-free alloys [18,20,31]. Planar glide of
dislocation in B2-free alloys can be attributed to the glide plane soft-
ening caused by either shearing of ??-carbides or interaction between
dislocations along with short-range order (SRO) [18,20,37]. The slip
band spacing measured in the present study at a particular strain in
28Mn0Ni alloy is comparable to that reported by Welsch et al. [20].
Although the deformation substructure evolution and associated strain
hardening have been reported for B2-free alloy, the same in the ??-matrix
in presence of B2 has not been studied in-detail. The slip band spacing
measured at a given strain (?? ∼ 0.15) in 28Mn0Ni alloy is ∼100–200 nm
whereas in 15Mn5Ni alloy it is ∼400–600 nm. Moreover, the slip bands
are homogeneously distributed in the 28Mn0Ni alloy as compared to in
15Mn5Ni alloy.
Slip band nucleation occurs when the critical resolved shear stress
exceeds the overall stress required to generate a Frank-Read source for
a given loop length and the friction stress. Once a slip band nucleates,
there will be a significant increase in dislocation density due to restricted
cross-slip activity. With further deformation, more dislocations can pile-
up within bands, exhaust the active source due to the force equilibrium
reached between the applied stress and the mutual repulsive stress be-
tween dislocations. A new source must be initiated to accommodate fur-
ther strain, thereby continuing the deformation process. This process
leads to dynamic slip band refinement. The slip band spacing also de
pends on the long-range stress field between bands. The nature of these
stress fields is governed by the number of dislocations piled-up within a
band [38]. The presence of coherent precipitates in the matrix can also
afect the stress fields and subsequently influence the microstructural
evolution according to their size and distribution. Kuhlmann-Wilsdorf
proposed that the dislocations are anchored in the presence of precip-
itates, resulting in a decrease in dislocation loop length which reduces
the number of active sources at given stress and thereby afecting the
slip band spacing [39]. Hence, it is expected that the slip bands can
be refined at a slower rate in the presence of non-shearable particles,
whereas shearable particles can enhance the slip band refinement rate.
The current study observed ??-carbides in 28Mn0Ni alloy to be smaller
and lesser in volume fraction and are sheared early during deformation.
This resulted in the observed finer slip band spacing as compared to the
15Mn5Ni alloy. It can be pointed out that the ??-carbides in 15Mn5Ni
alloy are not fully sheared across the specimen at low strain due to
their inhomogeneous distribution which result in non-uniform slip band
spacing. Apart from the ??-carbides, non-shearable B2 particles in the
15Mn5Ni alloy can also afect the slip band refinement. In the pres-
ence of B2, the active slip length reduced further, thereby leading to
high yield stress and contributing to a slower rate of slip band refine-
ment. Thus, the overall slip band spacing in 15Mn5Ni alloy decreases
at a much slower rate, leading to a lower strain hardening rate than
in 28Mn0Ni alloy. Apart from dynamic slip band refinement, annealing
twin-slip interaction is also prominent in 28Mn0Ni alloy. Thus, the dif-
ferences in strain-hardening characteristics of 28Mn0Ni and 15Mn5Ni
alloy can be attributed to various initial microstructural features such
as ??-carbides (its size and volume fraction), B2 (type, morphology and
orientation relationship with the matrix) and subsequent dislocation in-
teractions in the presence of these phases during deformation.
It is well-understood that the strain hardening exponent (n) is a mea-
sure of uniform strain that a polycrystalline material can accommodate.

<sup>•</sup> Rich B2 phase containing alloy exhibited the highest strength with
reduced ductility compared to the other alloys. The ??/B2 interface
played a critical role in controlling the strength and ductility of B2
containing alloys. A favourable orientation relationship (OR) be-
tween the ??-matrix and B2 facilitated slip transfer while the non-
favourable OR controlled the ductility by strain accumulation and
B2-cracking.
<sup>•</sup> Localised nanoindentation of ??-matrix and grains in B2 stringer
showed similar indentation response with B2 having a characteristic
‘pop-in’. This implies that during yield, co-deformation of ?? and B2
occurs along with slip transfer across favourable ??/B2 interfaces as
confirmed by transmission electron microscopy.
<sup>•</sup> The presence of both ??-carbides and B2 modified the dislocation
substructure evolution in austenite during deformation. Dislocations
were accumulated around ?? channels during yielding, which evolved
further as slip bands at higher strains followed by dynamic slip band
refinement. Slip band refinement in B2-free alloy was much faster
with uniform slip band spacing of 100–200 nm, whereas the pres-
ence of B2 limited the slip band refinement. This led to coarse and
inhomogeneous slip bands with spacing of 400–600 nm in 15Mn5N
alloy.
<sup>•</sup> At later stages of deformation, slip restriction at ??/B2 interface re-
sulted in high local re-orientation within a ??-grain surrounded by
B2 particles/stringers in 15Mn5Ni alloy as compared to the B2-free
28Mn0Ni alloy. Deformation twinning was also noticed in such re-
orientated grains which was absent in the B2-free 28Mn0Ni alloy.
The present study’s findings provide a critical understanding to eval-
uate microstructural modifications to enhance the mechanical proper-
ties of B2 containing low density steels.
